The story totally surprised me. It’s original, well-written, and kept me interested the whole way through. I actually cared about what was going on and wanted to see how things would play out.

As for the combat, I was expecting to be bored or confused but nope. The card system is way more fun and strategic than I expected. Even playing on Normal difficulty, I had to stop and really think about how to use my abilities and resources to get through some tough fights. It never felt unfair, just like the game was encouraging me to play smarter.
A bold, flawed, but ultimately fantastic game. Right up there with Insomniac's Spider-Man series and the Arkham series as some of the best comic-book video games of all time.

Your enjoyment of this game will depend on two things.

1) Do you like turn-based strategy games. If so, this is an easy recommend, as it's probably one of the most satisfying turn-based strategy combat systems ever made.
2) Do you have absolutely zero interested in Marvel. If so, it makes the game a lot better, because anyone actually familiar with these characters will have an ulcer from how out of character and weird most of them act. 

Frankly the roster would have been better if it stuck purely to lesser-known and younger Marvel characters, because seeing Wolverine or Blade or Venom happily telling you their tragic backstories the nanosecond you ask or Captain America starting a book club in order to get Captain Marvel to be her friend is extremely fuckin weird. 

All the original stuff with the main character is fine though. Lore is fun too. Easy recommend if you like these kinds of games.

Are you wondering if you should buy this? Well, I think it's not a terrible game, there are just a couple things to consider *breathes in*;

- Be prepared to watch a lot of cutscenes. A LOT. I hope you like that stuff. All the characters in this game feel like they want to go on forever about anything and everything (all of the time).

- The plot is generic at best. And we're talking Marvel games, I know that I shouldn't be particularly picky about this, but being able to be disappointed at the plot was somewhat surprising.

- Can we talk about video game writing and comedy? Ok. Why is it that most games feel like referencing popular culture somehow constitutes as humor? I spent 15 minutes playing this game before I got Iron Man referencing George Costanza from Seinfeld. No laughs were had, zero laughter, I was laughless.

- Midnight Suns one of [i]those[/i] games that wants to do a trillion things at the same time. The regular gameplay loop has you managing several card decks, upgrading said cards, collecting stuff in the hub area, decorating said hub, having all sorts of insignificant conversations with -I don't know- Blade?, using some combat facility for temporal bonuses, crafting shit, deploying heroes to side missions, etc., etc... And all of that happens before you can go on ONE battle. Then you come back and have to do it all again.

- Currencies, in all colors and shapes. You have credits, arcane keys, three types of essences, intel, compliments (!), gloss, blueprints (with varying levels of rarity), and reagents (also with several types). It's way too much, it seriously feels like an F2P mobile game.

- I'm sorry, but do we really need to hear about Spider-Man's secret origin each time Marvel licenses a product? Is that a clause in in The Contract? How many times more do you think we will have to hear this in our lives, because I think that 100% of Earth's population already knows this by now.

- I'm only 10 hours in, but I found that cosmetics are really scarce and pretty bland. Think "Tony Stark with a hoodie" and you already have a perfect mental image of how it looks. Sure, there's the premium (paid) content and the final "you maxed this social link" suit, but I think there's a chasm between those costumes and the free palette swaps that get thrown at you.

- Allow me to reiterate on the gameplay system overload that this game has. It features Persona-like affection and social link level, gifts, and "dates" included. It has XCOM-lite battles. It has deckbuilding. It has base management. It has exploring and collecting resources. It has alignment (dark/light), which is integrated into conversations. It has visual novel-ish storytelling. It has base decorating. It has character cosmetic customization. It has too many things.

- So, after 10 hours of gameplay, I'm still not sure I've unlocked every system, and that truly scares me.

- Somewhere, buried beneath layers upon layers of useless garbage, there's a pretty interesting game. I just think I shouldn't spend half of my gameplay time trying to find it.

I hate to give this a bad review. The game is fun, and honestly the perfect intersection of things I like. They took a lot of things that worked from Deck builders, strategy games like XCOM and Into the Breach, and covered the whole thing with a Marvel skin.

So why the bad review? The game is unforgivably broken in its current state.
Despite being well above recommended specs, when launched from the 2K launcher the game has terrible framerate issues with frequent freezes and stutters. Thankfully though, there are ways to circumvent launching with the 2K launcher which largely fixes these issues.
No, the far bigger issue is that the game seems to frequently crash when manually saving, and sometimes (But less often) when auto-saving too. This sucks, especially considering the game mostly auto-saves around battles, but not during the sometimes long Abbey sequences. Worse yet, when the game DOES crash on manual save, it does it before the save file is created, wiping out progress, and when reloaded it does not allow all the options you had before (Specifically hangout activities stop being available). Okay you think, maybe we can just rely on the autosave and just treat it like a game with forced "Save points"... except sometimes it also crashes on autosave, and now you've lost a very large amount of progress if you did any sort of Abbey activities.

So far I am marked as having played 11h, but I think 3-4 of those have been replaying sections of the game after it crashed on some sort of save.

The game also has other minor issues such as long loads at times, or audio temporarily going out, but the save crashes are by far the worst offender.
It's a shame because the game is excellent when it works, but the issues are infinitely more frustrating than the game is fun, so I would suggest skipping it until it works.

More RPG than strategy game, but with a healthy chunk of both genres, this is a different style of game to one you might expect coming from Firaxis, one tailored more towards immersing you in a world rather than flinging you at constant battles.

That's not to say there aren't battles aplenty to be had, because there are a LOT of them, but rather than bases and battles, the majority of the focus of this game seems to be on environment exploration and characters.

And I think it does those things pretty darn well.

-- Game Length --
Took me 120+ hours to play through my first playthrough, though that was a playthrough where I unlocked everything, maxed out every friendship, and got every achievement apart from full Dark points (as I had committed to a Light playthrough).

So there is plenty of content to engage with, but it's also a game you could probably breeze through in 20 to 30ish hours if you just focused down the main story and did little else.

-- Gameplay --
As for the gameplay, improving character stats and modding cards was addictive, it had a good curve of progression, and decent room for self expressing and experimentation. 

The fights themselves were ones that I never ended up getting bored of, even through all my hours of probably a bit too much grinding, and a shout out to the animation teams for the in-fight animations: The game is beautiful in combat at max settings and high FPS, though this does lead to a bit of an odd contrast with the quite clunky cutscene and dialogue animations, but that's forgivable enough.

The exploration back at the Abbey was surprisingly my main reason for coming back to the game during my first 40 - 50 hours of gameplay, I feel the game's captured that sense of eerie wonder that some early Harry Potter titles and Fable 1 managed to do quite well. 
Which in truth is probably my biggest surprise of the game, I did not expect so much of this game to be about exploration and mystery solving, nor did I then expect to find myself loving every minute of this side of the game (which I did).

-- The Writing --
It's strong in the character interactions, be it via the game's in-built fake social messaging system where you can read the characters talking with eachother about all the things going on in the game (both big and small), or via the hangouts and various conversations you can listen in on or join in in person.

It really does do a good job of making you feel like you're living with all these people, and I quite liked most of those people I shared the Abbey with, so it was a good time.

But it must be said that the writing takes a bit of a nose dive when it comes to the main plot.
Basically, nothing will surprise you if you've seen this kind of plot before, well, almost nothing, the second arc had some nice, admittedly small, curveballs in it.

But the plot gets you from points A to B, and allows the real good writing (the living with everyone at the Abbey) to exist within its literary casing well enough, so it's not the end of the world.

Though another thing worth noting is that the writing never makes an attempt to explain why Captain Marvel isn't just flying all your enemies up into space, or why you only send 3 Heroes out on a mission and the others just chill at home while the world is burning all around us, or why it takes Iron Man multiple missiles just to blow up a General Mission Objective glass container, or any of that power level stuff.

Obviously the answer to all these things is "it's so the video game can exist", but it's sad to see no attempt at an official explanation given for any of this, it's basically left up to player imagination to come up with their own headcanon explanations.

-- Overall Impression --
Definitely a game I'm glad I bought, and a new direction for Firaxis that I hope they pursue in future titles.

I was honestly pretty disappointed by vanilla XCOM 2, it felt quite uninspired to me at the time (though the later DLC expansions did a lot to make up for that), so seeing Firaxis try something new, both in terms of how they handle strategy gameplay, and in terms of overall game design (with this game's focus on exploration and characters) was a pretty cool thing to see.

This game's not perfect, but it's got a lot going for it, and it feels like a game the dev team wanted to make.

So played for a while (after reading the reviews) and, I have to say, as i often do these days; "I dont know what people are crying about!" - with regards to the game itself, the microtransactions are another thing, we'll get to that.

So, long story short: No, this is not a "dating sim", not even sure where that came from! Yes, you can raise/ lower affinity with your team but not sure what that has to do with dating, (there's a lot more to dating, kids!). Possibly because the friendship meter is represented by a heart? i dunno.

Also, yes there is a lot of non-combat stuff to do, much of it is actually optional but definitely encouraged. (the abbey grounds are immense!)

I actually enjoy strange and stark bickering, i think they got it spot on with their personalities (particularly stark). And always good to see Cpn. Marvel, my fav character in the mix!

All that aside, the game has grabbed me in a surprising way, (i don't play card games at all, usually avoid them tbh!)

Either way, i reckon you could do a lot worse than this, it's a solid title that really scratches my superhero itch, it's immersive character interactions and strategic battles will keep you entertained for many hours and I for one am loving every one so far! 8.5/10 (would be 9 if they'd included Star girl! I mean, she's magical right?)

Marvel’s Midnight Suns is an inventive tactical RPG that takes the familiar world of Marvel superheroes and pushes it into supernatural territory filled with demons, dark magic, ancient prophecies, and apocalyptic threats. Developed by Firaxis Games and published by 2K, it avoids becoming another conventional superhero action game by combining turn-based tactical battles with card-based abilities, character relationships, exploration, and extensive progression. The combination sounds unusual, but the different systems fit together surprisingly well and give the game an identity distinct from most other Marvel adaptations.

The campaign places players in control of the Hunter, a customizable demon slayer resurrected to confront Lilith, the Mother of Demons. Rather than simply controlling established Marvel characters through a familiar comic-book storyline, players become part of the team through an original protagonist. The Hunter can be customized and developed throughout the campaign, while interactions with other heroes gradually establish the character as more than a convenient player avatar. The supernatural premise also gives less commonly explored aspects of Marvel's universe considerable attention, creating a darker atmosphere without completely abandoning the humor and personality associated with its heroes.

Combat is the strongest part of the experience. Each hero brings a small customized deck of ability cards into battle, and the available hand determines which attacks, defensive abilities, support powers, and special techniques can be performed. Cards consume or generate resources, while redraws and limited movement opportunities introduce additional decisions. Instead of simply selecting the strongest attack every turn, players must determine how to extract maximum value from the abilities currently available.

Environmental interaction adds another layer of strategy. Enemies can be knocked into objects, hazards, or one another, while various pieces of scenery can become improvised weapons. Positioning consequently matters even though the game does not rely on a traditional tactical grid. Knocking one opponent into another can damage both, while carefully using environmental attacks can eliminate weaker enemies without wasting valuable cards. The result is combat that regularly feels like solving a tactical puzzle while simultaneously delivering the exaggerated spectacle expected from superhero battles.

Hero variety further strengthens the system. Characters are not interchangeable collections of powerful attacks. Their abilities encourage noticeably different approaches, and successful squads are often built around complementary strengths. Some heroes excel at absorbing punishment or protecting teammates, others specialize in raw damage, and several provide valuable support or battlefield manipulation. Deck customization becomes increasingly important as additional cards, upgrades, and modifications become available. Experimenting with different combinations is one of the game's greatest pleasures because improving a deck can fundamentally change how efficiently a hero performs.

The Abbey provides the other major half of the experience. Between missions, the Hunter can explore the headquarters and surrounding grounds, participate in activities, uncover mysteries, improve abilities, gather resources, and spend time with other characters. This transforms the campaign into something closer to a character-focused RPG than a straightforward sequence of tactical missions. Exploration also introduces secrets and optional discoveries that reward players who enjoy investigating environments rather than immediately jumping into the next battle.

Friendship mechanics play a significant role in progression. Conversations, activities, gifts, and other interactions can strengthen relationships with individual heroes. These sequences reveal more personal sides of famous characters who otherwise spend much of their time fighting supernatural enemies. Building relationships can also produce gameplay benefits, meaning that the social system is connected to progression rather than existing purely as optional dialogue.

This emphasis on relationships will not appeal equally to everyone. Players expecting nonstop tactical combat may find the amount of conversation and downtime excessive. Some exchanges can feel lengthy, and the constant transition between social activities, exploration, preparation, and combat occasionally weakens the urgency of the central supernatural crisis. The tone can also shift rapidly between serious discussions about catastrophic threats and comparatively casual conversations around the Abbey. Players who enjoy character-driven RPGs are likely to appreciate these sections considerably more than those interested exclusively in strategy.

Visually, the game successfully combines superhero spectacle with supernatural imagery. Powers are accompanied by satisfying effects and animations, while the darker environments complement the occult direction of the story. The combat presentation is particularly effective when powerful abilities send enemies flying across arenas or trigger elaborate attacks. Character models and conversational animations are less consistently impressive, but the overall presentation remains strong enough to support the lengthy campaign.

Progression provides plenty of reasons to continue experimenting. Improving cards, refining decks, developing friendships, strengthening the Hunter, researching upgrades, and discovering new tactical combinations create multiple interconnected progression paths. This makes the experience particularly satisfying for players who enjoy gradually transforming an initially modest collection of abilities into highly efficient character builds. There is enough strategic flexibility to encourage different team compositions rather than forcing one universally superior squad.

On Steam Deck, Marvel’s Midnight Suns is officially classified as Playable rather than Verified. This means it can be played on Valve's handheld, but users should expect some compromises or aspects that do not fully satisfy the requirements for the highest compatibility rating. Full controller support makes the fundamental interface and turn-based combat naturally suitable for handheld play. Its mission-based structure is also a good conceptual match for portable sessions, although players prioritizing completely seamless Steam Deck integration should keep the Playable classification in mind.

There are some drawbacks beyond pacing. Mission structures and environments can become familiar over a long campaign, while players who dislike card mechanics may struggle to appreciate the core combat regardless of its strategic depth. The game also includes in-game purchases and third-party DRM. Nevertheless, these concerns do not overshadow the strength of its central tactical design.

Marvel’s Midnight Suns ultimately succeeds by taking creative risks with an enormously recognizable superhero property. Its mixture of deckbuilding, turn-based strategy, environmental combat, exploration, friendships, customization, and supernatural storytelling creates an experience with substantially more depth than a straightforward superhero action game. The slower social sections and occasional repetition prevent it from being universally appealing, but players who enjoy tactical experimentation and character-focused RPG progression will find an unusually rich adventure.

Rating: 9/10

It's a shame that this game was a flop. If I were to blame anything at a glance, it would be the game's banner. If you are familiar with Marvel, you don't need to be shown the heroes staring at you.

gameplay is fun. But most of the time you're walking around a castle skipping terrible dialogue. I think I had 1 hours of missions and the rest was talking to people and walking through the open world menu.

XCOM + Mass Effect + Slay The Spire wrapped in the Marvel magic. What's not to like?

[h1] Marvel Battle Waifu Dress-Up Simulator 2022 is Pretty Great! [/h1]

No seriously. Lots of mixed reviews but I've been playing this thing as of time of posting this for like 12 hours. Is it perfect? No, but that's mainly due to technical issues right now. I'm not going to give a super-duper in depth report on every little thing, I'm just going to highlight the stuff that I find the best (and worst) and whatnot. Sound and graphics are fine, I'm not running a rig you'd find at NASA or MIT here. 

*Win 10
*Ryzen 7 3700x
*64gb RAM
*RTX 2060

[b]The Good[/b]
--The Power Fantasy--
Teaming up with earth's mightiest heroes (and some of the less than mightiest) has never been more fun, this time with a self-insert OC of your choosing. Knocking around Hydra troopers like rag dolls to smash into each other or explosive barrels or NYC mailboxes feels amazing. 1 HP minions that blow away like dust in the wind to set up chain attacks or environmental combos make you feel super powerful, while whittling down chunkier enemies is less of a chore (so far) than one might imagine, due to the amount of stuff you can play with on a given battlefield. So long as you don't use it all up too quickly! The big flashy Heroic attacks feel amazing and flashy, too! The higher-tier ones definitely even more! [spoiler] Like Ghost Rider's ghost ridin' and Miss Marvel's particle mega beam cannon. [/spoiler]

--The Combat--
Coming from having played the more recent XCOM games as well as Phoenix Point, I knew more or less what I was getting into. I won't rehash what's above but the change from the slow deliberate cover-to-cover hopping and Hail Mary long shot hopes and dreams being shattered to in your face superhero explosions is definitely [i]a change[/i] but it suits the theme. If you temper expectations as to [i]how[/i] the combat plays out versus the much slower, more deliberate offerings in the genre you'll enjoy it a lot because the more cinematic approach here does the entire thing a lot of justice. We want to see Iron Man blasting Hyda goons with his palm repulsors, not hiding behind a waist-high wall and missing Hydra Bob with a 95% chance to hit.

Some folks might seriously dislike the randomness of the card system but you get a chance for a couple of redraws per turn, and the abilities always do what they say they'll do with no chance of failure. So while it may make things more predictable, the card element adds some of that randomness back in which represents the chaos of a comic-style brawl.

--The Banter--

Marvel's Midnight Suns is a turn-based strategy / deckbuilding hybrid that brings together some of the most popular characters from the similarly-named comics alongside a wide ensemble of lesser known superheroes in order to fight an increasingly popular villain of today's gaming world: Lilith, the Mother of All Demons. As such, the game leans heavily into eldritch horror and magical elements, something rather rare for a Marvel game, while still retaining some tech elements most often delivered by Iron Man, Spider-Man or Bobby Reyes.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2903957113

The Marvel gang acts as a supporting cast for the game’s true protagonist - the Hunter - whose customizable nature enables you to explore a number of different builds depending on the alignment, collar and card decisions you make along the way. Each day you choose to go on a mission, but there’s never any forced progression (you can choose to do an infinite number of secondary missions and not progress the story if you prefer), which enables you to explore the hundreds of optional conversations, arcane chests, mysteries and optional activities at your own pace. 

During your adventures, you will run into iconic villains like Venom or Sabretooth, corrupted by cosmic horror influences and making a recurring appearance as minibosses. You will help heroes along the way and unlock them as playable characters, each with their own synergies and specialties. The game’s physical mechanics, environment, buffs and debuffs will seem a bit shallow compared to more hardcore TCG hybrids like Slay the Spire, but provide a few stimulating concepts to play with for newcomers the genre. Regardless of whether you are a min-maxer or just a casual marvel collectionist taking a dip into another yarn featuring their favorite characters, it will take you well over 50 hours to finish the game’s story. Along the way, you will find quite a few satisfying eureka moments, whether it’s building up a perfect engine of Quick cards into a board-clearing Heroic or shoving a fragile opponent into the perfect chain reaction. For a while, you will even be mesmerized by how every card has a corresponding animation, the more powerful ones displaying impressive cinematics that show Marvel heavy hitters go into full Super Sayan mode.

Positioning your heroes correctly, using explosives and props for area attacks after having exhausted your card-based relocators will sometimes prove critical to winning engagements, particularly on the higher difficulty levels on the game’s sliding scale (the difficulty can be adjusted at any time for varying rewards and challenges). While the general missions fall into a number of formulaic types, the storyline quests typically follow a two-phase format with sometimes surprising requests that alter your playstyle completely.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2903957765

While the main game takes a rather minimalistic approach in regards to the size and scope of each battle, you'll only be spending about a third of your time solving the chess-like puzzles that make up the main story. Another third will be spent clearing up general-type missions in order to stock up on cards, essences, credits and intel, and perhaps more interestingly the final third will be spent exploring the grounds around your base, fittingly called the Abbey for all its arcane backstories and collectibles. This exploratory part of the game resembles the Krypt mode in Mortal Kombat somewhat, as you will unlock abilities and secrets that allow you to access new areas and gradually uncover the mysteries laid throughout. Words of Power will open up new areas and sidequests will have you returning later in the evening for specific nocturnal triggers. 

You can also collect reagents such as plants or mushrooms that you can craft consumables with, and at one point you will have built this sort of ritual where you access daily features in a specific order before advancing the time and launching the next mission. What’s even better, the game’s research / upgrade system encourages you to use the entire roster of heroes on rotation, in order to unlock global bonuses. Gloss functions as a currency for cosmetics: the Hunter’s numerous customizable helmets, tattoos and make-up options, the bedroom upgrades and frames and finally the plethora of paintings you can collect and hang up in frames inside the mansion’s many rooms.

Fans of the X-COM games will be happy to hear that there's a heavy base progression element, rich with crafting options, hero customization and secondary activities, and there's an almost inexorable amount of dialogue featuring any and all characters of the Marvel Universe. Building up your relationships unlocks passive skills, bonuses and eventually allows you to complete challenges to unlock each hero's strongest card and a special Midnight Sun costume.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2903956618

Sadly, however, even if it’s a long haul, I can’t honestly say Midnight Suns has any replayability value. You’ll unlock pretty much everything the game has to show you before the final mission, and unless you’re keen on getting the opposing alignment achievement, you won’t have to do much farming outside of the game’s natural playcycle either. Another minor flaw it has that some general missions have a flawed design, where they have you kill a certain number of enemies but don’t spawn enough enemies and there are minor graphical glitches every now and then, yet nothing major. 

The voice acting is also hit and miss, and because of the ocean of dialogue there’s bound to be a lot of filler; I found myself skipping the audio interpretation and just reading the subtitles as quickly as I could on secondary banter towards the end. While there is an incentive to engage characters in secondary dialogue, mostly because of friendship and alignment gains, and a big portion of it is made of interesting takes all of these iconic do-gooders have on anything from literature to old movies, I have to admit there are a number of scenes and exchanges that really feel like filler.

Marvel’s Midnight Suns is one of the better games I played this year, and I wholeheartedly recommend it to anyone who is in the mood for a turn-based ride through a superhero-themed TCG. Know however that while there is 50-100 hours worth of content, depending on your pace, you will most likely not replay this title once you’re done.

I'd read and watched reviews ahead of time that suggested the combat was great and the story/writing/characters were incredibly bland. They mostly said, "Play it for the combat, skip the dialogue." I was satisfied enough with some of the initial writing and cut-scenes but figured it would wear off quickly. Instead, my appreciation has actually GROWN for the interactions, conversations, and many of the little things I get to (and have to) do around the abbey (base). Sometimes they're bland and I just can't care, but they're often revealing and interesting, or hilarious, or surprising.

You get tonnnnns of dialogue options and choices throughout the game, usually at least a few within each in-game day. While not groundbreaking and hyper-innovative, I've been pleasantly surprised by one main factor - the outcomes aren't obvious. I've played games where I hated that quality, but here I enjoy it (with some mild frustration, much like real life convos). It's not as simple as "good/bad" choices and options, which you might assume with the "light/dark" quality, but that seems to be more "pessimistic/optimistic" than anything else. And the different characters react very differently to your choices, often in ways you have to learn as you continue to develop relationships with them via convos.

Finally, combat is ridiculously good. Like, it has no business being this good. It might illegal. Could just be my perspective, but this is setting a new bar for tactical turn-based combat for me. Not by leaps and bounds, but it's just absolutely hot and constantly makes me hungry for a lot more. Each character plays REALLY differently, to a surprising and satisfactory degree. This becomes more and more obvious as the game goes on and you continue to evolve cards and unlock new ones; you customize the deck for each character to fit your flavor and the team dynamics you enjoy the most. The devs miraculously navigate the tension between 1) keeping the characters true to their comic history, 2) allow each to be entirely unique, and, most importantly here, 3) allow you to (moderately) make each of them your own in terms of play style (deck customization and actual in-combat play choices).

Get it. Play it. Love it.

Midnight Suns is one of those games that I was unsure about, as the genre (Turn-Based Deck-Building Strategy) wasn't something I played before. However I gotta say, it's rather spectacular, entertaining and opened up a whole new avenue of games for me to try.
Here's a Pros & Cons list.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
+ Customisable main character. Ability to customise team-mate outfits. There is a fair amount of customising in this game.
+ Wide Variety of Heroes / Anti-Heroes to choose from. [i](Iron Man, Ghost Rider, Deadpool, Blade, Storm & Spider-Man to name a few).[/i] With plenty of villains to match.
+ Exploration - Before & after mission exploration, allowing you to learn some lore, gain collectables, improve friendship levels with other heroes & improve heroes abilities and outfits.
+ Plenty of abilities, unique to each hero, allowing you to find your perfect play-style.
+ Voice acting is top notch.
+ Visually pleasing to look at.
+ Great story, decent writing. Deadpool & Blade is a duo I never realised I needed until I played this. Combines gravitas with comedy rather well.

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
- Noticeable FPS drops in certain areas [i](The Abbey to The Yard / The Abbey to The Forge areas).[/i] Mostly smooth everywhere else.
- Certain dialogues overlap. (Listening to 2 different people talk at the same time). Rather sporadic when it occurs.
- Only one mission per in-game day. It'd be nice if I can do 2-3 missions a day before having my heroes rest. Instead, you're forced to rest after 1 mission. 
- Pricing. The best edition which includes the season pass & a few hero customisation options, is a bit pricey at £90.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Overall, as a game that's introduced me to a whole new genre of games, I'd say it's definitely worth playing.
Although with how pricey the best edition is, I'd recommend buying it on a discount of 40%.
8/10 worth it!
